explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Pilate asks Jesus, "Are You the King of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11). Jesus replies, "You have said so." Out of every title Pilate could have started with, he went straight for the big one.

I see why that came to mind, since priests are all over this scene. But the chief priests are the ones doing the accusing here (Matthew 27:12). Pilate's question is "Are You the King of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11). Nobody asks Jesus about being a high priest.

That title sounds like it could be in this trial, but Pilate never says it. He asks, "Are You the King of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11). Jesus answers, "You have said so." So it's King, friend, and that's the title the whole scene starts with.

I get why you'd expect it, since most of us would be arguing by the second accusation. But the text says the opposite. When the chief priests and elders accuse Him, "He gave no answer" (Matthew 27:12). Jesus doesn't argue back at all.

Right, baker. While the chief priests and elders accuse Him, "He gave no answer" (Matthew 27:12). No arguing and no defending. I can barely stay quiet when someone looks at my cookies funny, so this one amazes me.

Yes, friend. Jesus gave no answer, "not even to a single charge, much to the governor's amazement" (Matthew 27:14). I think that silence was the loudest thing in the room. I'd have needed to sit down.

Silence can make a person mad, so I see the thinking. But the text names a different reaction. Jesus gave no answer "much to the governor's amazement" (Matthew 27:14). Pilate is amazed, and anger isn't mentioned.

The text doesn't send Pilate anywhere. Jesus gave no answer "much to the governor's amazement" (Matthew 27:14). A few verses later, Pilate is still right there asking the crowd questions (Matthew 27:17). He stays put and stays amazed.

That's it. "Now it was the governor's custom at the feast to release to the crowd a prisoner of their choosing" (Matthew 27:15). The crowd gets to choose, and that matters a lot in the next verses. Hold onto that.

Soldiers are a fair guess when a governor is in the room. But the custom is about someone being let go, and the text says what kind of person. The governor releases "a prisoner of their choosing" (Matthew 27:15). The crowd picks, and it's a prisoner.

Close to the right kind of person, but not the one. The text says it was the governor's custom "to release to the crowd a prisoner of their choosing" (Matthew 27:15). A servant isn't part of this custom. Only a prisoner is.

You got it, baker. Matthew says Pilate "knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him" (Matthew 27:18). The text tells us what Pilate knew, and it doesn't say what they were envious of. So we'll leave that open too.

Fear is a common reason for people to do things, so I see the thinking. But Matthew gives a different one. Pilate "knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him" (Matthew 27:18). Envy is the word the text uses.
That sounds neat and official, friend, but it isn't what the text says. Pilate "knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him" (Matthew 27:18). Envy is the reason Matthew gives.

explanations.answer: Have nothing to do with that innocent man
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Her message says, "Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him" (Matthew 27:19). She calls Jesus innocent, plain and simple. That message lands right in the middle of the trial.

explanations.answer: Let the chief priests decide what to do
explanations.explanation: That would hand the whole thing to the accusers, and her message does the opposite. She says, "Have nothing to do with that innocent man" (Matthew 27:19). The chief priests aren't even mentioned in her message. She's talking about Jesus.

explanations.answer: Send that man back home to Galilee
explanations.explanation: Galilee never comes up in her message. What she says is, "Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him" (Matthew 27:19). She calls Him innocent and tells Pilate to stay out of it.

That's right, friend. She writes, "I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him" (Matthew 27:19). The text gives us the dream and the suffering, and it doesn't say more about the dream. So I'll leave it right there.

Actually, the text says she did. Her message says, "I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him" (Matthew 27:19). That's in her own words, sent to Pilate while he sat on the judgment seat. The dream is part of why she calls Jesus an innocent man.

explanations.answer: Barabbas freed and Jesus put to death
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "The chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death" (Matthew 27:20). This is a heavy turn. I think it hurts to see the crowd shift like that.

explanations.answer: Jesus freed and Barabbas kept locked up
explanations.explanation: That's the flip side of what happens, friend. The text says the chief priests and elders "persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death" (Matthew 27:20). So it's Barabbas who gets asked for, and Jesus who is asked to be put to death. I think this part is heavy.

explanations.answer: Jesus sent to Herod to be judged
explanations.explanation: Herod doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. What the text says is that the chief priests and elders "persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death" (Matthew 27:20). The request is about Barabbas and about Jesus' death. It's a heavy moment, friend.

Yes, baker. Pilate asks, "What then should I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" and "They all answered, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:22). I think this one hurts, and it's okay to feel that. There's more to this story.

I wish it had gone that way, friend, but that's not what the text says. They all answered, "Crucify Him!" (Matthew 27:22). Release was Pilate's custom with the prisoner they chose, and they chose Barabbas (Matthew 27:15, 21). This part is heavy.
That's a gentle word, and I wish it were the one. But the text says they all answered, "Crucify Him!" (Matthew 27:22). That's the crowd's answer to Pilate. It's a hard verse to read.

I wish that were the case, but the text says no. Pilate asks, "Why? What evil has He done?" and the crowd "shouted all the louder, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:23). Louder, not quieter. This is a heavy moment.

That's right, baker. Pilate asks, "Why? What evil has He done?" and they "shouted all the louder, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:23). The question doesn't quiet them. It's a hard verse, and the crowd gets louder.

That's what he does, friend. Pilate "took water and washed his hands before the crowd" (Matthew 27:24). Then he says, "I am innocent of this man's blood." The text doesn't say more about why he did it, so I'll leave it there.
That would be a dramatic move, but the text doesn't have Pilate do it. He "took water and washed his hands before the crowd" (Matthew 27:24). It's water and his hands, not a robe.

A riot is breaking out, so I see why you'd think of soldiers. But the text doesn't say he sends any. It says Pilate "took water and washed his hands before the crowd" (Matthew 27:24). That's what he does.

Yes, that's the word, baker. Pilate says, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24). Those are his words about himself. His wife had already called Jesus "that innocent man" (Matthew 27:19).

That's the one, friend. Pilate tells the crowd, "You bear the responsibility" (Matthew 27:24). He says it right after saying he's innocent of this man's blood. It's the second blank, and it matches his own words.
That's the opposite of what Pilate says. His words are, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24). So "innocent" is the word that fills the first blank. "Guilty" isn't in his mouth here.

That's a close cousin of the right word, but it's not the one Pilate uses. He tells the crowd, "You bear the responsibility" (Matthew 27:24). Responsibility is the word Matthew records. Punishment doesn't show up in his words.
That's a feeling word, and Pilate doesn't use it here. He says, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24). Innocent is his word for the first blank. The text doesn't tell us about shame.

That's right, baker. Matthew says, "he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified" (Matthew 27:26). I think this one hurts, and I won't dress it up. We'll stay with it a moment and keep going.
That isn't what the text says, friend. It says Pilate "had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified" (Matthew 27:26). Chains aren't mentioned in this verse. This is a heavy one.
Prison isn't part of this verse. Matthew says Pilate "had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified" (Matthew 27:26). I think it's a hard verse to read, and that's okay.
